terms.grammar: relative pronoun: gender and number from the word it refers to, case from its own clause
evidence: Catull. 3.5: quem plūs illa oculīs suīs amābat
Phaedr. 1 prol. 1: Aesōpus auctor quam māteriam repperit
terms.comment: English may leave the relative out (“the boat you see”); Latin never does. Its genitive cujus, quōrum, quārum is “whose”, its dative cui, quibus “to whom”. At the head of a sentence it links back where English says “and he”, “and this”: quā lēctā, and when I had read it (Cic. Att. 12.1.2).

phrases.latin: passer mortuus est meae puellae, passer, dēliciae meae puellae, quem plūs illa oculīs suīs amābat
phrases.english: my girl’s sparrow is dead, the sparrow, my girl’s delight, whom she loved more than her own eyes

phrases.latin: Aesōpus auctor quam māteriam repperit, hanc ego polīvī versibus sēnāriīs
phrases.english: the material that Aesop the author found, I have polished in iambic verse

phrases.latin: cum complicārem hanc epistulam, noctuābundus ad mē vēnit cum epistulā tuā tabellārius; quā lēctā dē Atticae febriculā scīlicet valdē doluī.
phrases.english: As I was folding this letter, the courier came to me by night with yours; when I had read it, I was of course very sorry about Attica’s touch of fever.

phrases.latin: vīvitur parvō bene, cui paternum splendet in mēnsā tenuī salīnum
phrases.english: he lives well on little whose father’s salt-cellar shines on his plain table

phrases.latin: aper … pilleātus, ē cujus dentibus sportellae dēpendēbant duae palmulīs textae
phrases.english: a boar wearing a freedman’s cap, from whose tusks hung two little baskets woven of palm
